Ball Clock

Twelve black balls on thin rods radiate from a white disc: the atomic starburst of 1950s graphics turned into a wall clock.

Source
Art Institute of Chicago: Ball Clock, 1999.678
Creator
Irving Harper, George Nelson Associates
Made
1948–69 (Art Institute of Chicago)
Style
Mid-century modern (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Atomic, playful, optimistic
Evidence
Inspected, in the scratchpad only, the Art Institute of Chicago photograph of 1999.678 at 843 × 671 px (the largest size served for this in-copyright object), a frontal view on gray. Not stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The Art Institute of Chicago dates the clock 1948–69 and credits Irving Harper (1916–2015) and George Nelson Associates, manufactured by Herman Miller Inc.; materials chrome, black enameled metal, and ebonized wood; Orbit Fund. AIC 1999.678.

The museum’s text places it in the Chronopak series of electric clocks that Harper designed at George Nelson Associates and says that, though abstract, it “suggests both the structure of the atom and the iconic asterisk symbol that abounded in the 1950s”. AIC.

Observed

  • Twelve black spheres sit at the ends of thin metal rods that radiate evenly from a central white disc.
  • The hands are black: the hour hand ends in a triangle and the minute hand in a thin lozenge shape. There are no numerals.
  • The photograph shows the clock straight on against a flat gray background.

Why it belongs

The clock is the three-dimensional version of the starburst and ball-and-stick motifs in 1950s prints: a circle, radial lines, and dots with nothing else.

Borrow

Use a ring of dots on thin radial lines around a plain disc as a starburst motif.

Give pointers or markers simple geometric ends: a triangle, a lozenge, a circle.
